themeName: Theme 2: The UK Economy - Performance and Policies

cards.front: Define GDP, and distinguish actual from potential growth.
cards.back:
Gross Domestic Product — the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given year: the primary measure of economic activity.

Actual growth is a rise in real GDP — producing more than last year. Potential growth is a rise in productive capacity — what the economy could produce at full employment.

cards.front: State the expenditure approach to measuring GDP.
cards.back: Consumption + Investment + Government spending + Net exports. The income approach — summing wages, rent, interest and profit — must reach the same total, because every pound spent is a pound of income for someone.
cards.formulaHtml: GDP=C+I+G+(X−M)GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)GDP=C+I+G+(X−M)

cards.front: Distinguish real vs nominal GDP, total vs per capita, and define GNI.
cards.back:
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, showing the true change in the volume of output — the measure of growth (value vs volume). GDP per capita divides real GDP by population — the better guide to average living standards.

GNI — GDP plus net income from abroad, such as profits sent home by citizens overseas minus income flowing out to foreign owners.

cards.front: What are purchasing power parities (PPPs), and why are they used?
cards.back:
PPP — a conversion factor that accounts for differences in the cost of living between countries, adjusting income figures to show how much a standard basket of goods can be bought locally.

PPP-adjusted figures make international comparisons of real living standards meaningful: £1,000 buys far more in some countries than others, so raw exchange-rate conversions mislead.

cards.front: Evaluate the limitations of GDP for comparing living standards, and the national happiness evidence.
cards.back:
GDP per capita masks inequality; excludes unpaid work, leisure and environmental quality; counts welfare-reducing 'bads' like pollution clean-up; struggles with quality improvements; and misses the informal economy.

Hence the spec's interest in national wellbeing: the UK measures subjective happiness alongside GDP, and rising real incomes raise reported happiness only weakly beyond a point.

cards.front: Define inflation, deflation and disinflation.
cards.back:
Inflation — a sustained increase in the general/average price level of goods and services in an economy.

Deflation — a sustained decrease in the general price level: a negative inflation rate. Disinflation — a decrease in the rate of inflation: prices still rising, but more slowly.

cards.front: How is UK inflation measured with the CPI? State the inflation-rate formula.
cards.back: A representative basket of around 700 goods and services, weighted by each item's share of household spending, is priced monthly; the basket's cost is expressed as an index against a base year set to 100. The Bank of England's target is CPI inflation of 2%.
cards.formulaHtml: Inflation rate=CPIyear 2−CPIyear 1CPIyear 1×100\text{Inflation rate} = \frac{\text{CPI}_{\text{year 2}} - \text{CPI}_{\text{year 1}}}{\text{CPI}_{\text{year 1}}} \times 100Inflation rate=CPIyear 1​CPIyear 2​−CPIyear 1​​×100

cards.front: A basket costs £480 in the 2023 base year, £504 in 2024 and £524.16 in 2025. Calculate the CPI for each year and the inflation rate for 2024 and 2025.
cards.back:
CPI: 2023 = 100; 2024 = 504 ÷ 480 × 100 = 105; 2025 = 524.16 ÷ 480 × 100 = 109.2

Inflation 2024 = (105 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 5%

Inflation 2025 = (109.2 − 105) ÷ 105 × 100 = 4%

Inflation fell yet the basket still costs more — disinflation, not deflation. Each year's rate is measured against the previous year's index, not the base year.

cards.front: State the limitations of the CPI, and how the RPI differs.
cards.back:
CPI's average basket may not represent particular households (pensioners, students); it ignores regional variation; it lags quality improvements and consumers' substitution to cheaper alternatives; and it rests on sample surveys.

RPI includes housing costs such as mortgage interest and council tax, generally yields a higher rate, and is not the UK's official target measure.

cards.front: Explain the three causes of inflation in the Edexcel specification.
cards.back:
Demand-pull — anything raising C, I, G or X−M shifts AD right and pulls the price level up. Cost-push — higher production costs (commodity prices, wages, indirect taxes, a weaker currency) shift SRAS left, raising prices while cutting output.

Money supply growth — excessive growth (e.g. quantitative easing) fuels both: cheaper borrowing boosts spending, and a depreciating currency raises import costs. A wage-price spiral can then sustain inflation after the original cause fades.

cards.front: Evaluate the effects of inflation on consumers, firms, the government and workers.
cards.back:
Consumers — real incomes and the value of savings erode, hitting living standards. Firms — uncertainty discourages investment, higher inflation than trading partners erodes international competitiveness, and menu costs mount.

Government — index-linked pensions and benefits cost more, widening the deficit. Workers — real wages fall unless pay keeps pace, prompting the wage demands that can spiral.

cards.front: Define unemployed, the labour force and economically inactive.
cards.back:
Unemployed — an individual of working age who is without work, but is willing and able to work, and is actively seeking employment.

Labour force — those in employment plus the unemployed actively seeking work. Economically inactive — working-age people not seeking work: full-time students, early retirees, the long-term sick, discouraged workers.

cards.front: A working-age population of 40 million has 26m in employment, 2m unemployed and 12m economically inactive. Calculate the unemployment rate and the employment rate.
cards.back:
Labour force = 26m + 2m = 28m

Unemployment rate = 2 ÷ 28 × 100 = 7.1%

Employment rate = 26 ÷ 40 × 100 = 65%

The two rates use different denominators — the labour force versus the whole working-age population — which is why they do not sum to 100%: the 12 million inactive appear in neither.

cards.front: Contrast the UK's two measures of unemployment.
cards.back:
ILO / Labour Force Survey — the internationally comparable household survey: unemployed means without work, available to start within two weeks, and actively seeking in the last four.

Claimant Count — the number claiming unemployment-related benefits such as Jobseeker's Allowance. Usually lower than the LFS, since not all unemployed people claim.

cards.front: Name and define the five causes of unemployment in the Edexcel specification.
cards.back:
• Structural — skills mismatch as industries decline or technology shifts (coal mining regions).
  • Cyclical (demand-deficient) — a lack of aggregate demand in downturns (2008).
  • Frictional — short spells between jobs.
  • Seasonal — demand for labour varies through the year (ski instructors in summer).
  • Real wage inflexibility — wages held above the market-clearing level create excess labour supply.

cards.front: Define underemployment, and distinguish it from unemployment.
cards.back:
Underemployment — when workers are in jobs that underutilise their skills, or want to work more hours than they do — a qualified teacher working part-time as a barista.

Unlike the unemployed they have work, so they appear in the employment figures — a waste of productive potential hidden inside the statistics.

cards.front: Evaluate the effects of unemployment, and the significance of migration and skills.
cards.back:
Individuals — lower incomes and living standards, skills erode, health suffers. Government and society — lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending widen the deficit; social costs rise. Firms — weaker sales, though a larger labour pool can lower hiring costs.

Migration cuts unemployment where migrants fill shortages, and migrants' spending creates jobs; competition can raise unemployment in particular low-skilled sectors. Skills determine who escapes structural unemployment.

cards.front: Define the balance of payments, and name its three accounts.
cards.back:
Balance of payments — a record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. It must always balance: total credits equal total debits.

Current account — trade and income flows. Capital account — capital transfers and non-produced assets (small, often ignored). Financial account — cross-border investment flows (FDI, portfolio investment, reserves), which finance the current account balance.

cards.front: Name the four components of the current account.
cards.back:
• Trade in goods (visible balance) — exports credit, imports debit.
  • Trade in services (invisible balance) — banking, tourism, insurance.
  • Primary income — net investment income: dividends, interest, FDI profits.
  • Secondary income — net transfers with nothing exchanged: aid, pensions, remittances.

cards.front: Goods: credits £320bn, debits £410bn. Services: £290bn, £210bn. Primary income: £95bn, £120bn. Secondary income: £20bn, £35bn. Calculate the current account balance.
cards.back:
Goods: 320 − 410 = −£90bn

Services: 290 − 210 = +£80bn

Primary income: 95 − 120 = −£25bn; secondary income: 20 − 35 = −£15bn

Balance = −90 + 80 − 25 − 15 = −£50bn deficit. The services surplus partly offsets the goods deficit — quoting goods alone would overstate the deficit by £40bn.

cards.front: What causes a current account deficit, and how does correcting one conflict with other objectives?
cards.back:
Causes: high consumer spending and low saving pulling in imports; weak competitiveness and low productivity; a strong currency; slowdown in export markets; structural issues such as deindustrialisation.

Corrections trade off against other objectives — cutting demand through fiscal or monetary tightening slows growth and raises unemployment; supply-side improvement works but slowly and at a cost. Economies are interconnected through trade, so one country's deficit is another's surplus.

cards.front: Define aggregate demand, and explain why the AD curve slopes downward.
cards.back:
Aggregate demand — the total demand for all goods and services in an economy at a given average price level and in a given time period.

It slopes downward because a lower price level: raises the real value of money (wealth effect); lowers interest rates, encouraging borrowing (interest rate effect); and makes exports cheaper and imports dearer (international trade effect).

cards.front: State the components of aggregate demand.
cards.back: C — consumption: household spending on goods and services. I — investment: firms' spending on capital goods. G — government spending on state-provided goods and services, excluding transfer payments such as benefits. (X − M) — exports minus imports.
cards.formulaHtml: AD=C+I+G+(X−M)AD = C + I + G + (X - M)AD=C+I+G+(X−M)

cards.front: Rank the components of AD by relative importance in the UK.
cards.back:
• Consumption — around 60%, the largest component, so consumer confidence and incomes move AD most.
  • Government spending — around 25%, set by fiscal policy.
  • Investment — around 14%, the most volatile component.
  • Net exports — small and often negative, roughly 1% or less.

cards.front: C = £1,200bn, I = £280bn, G = £500bn, X = £640bn, M = £660bn. Calculate aggregate demand.
cards.back:
AD = 1,200 + 280 + 500 + (640 − 660) = £1,960bn

Net trade is negative (−£20bn) because imports exceed exports, so it is subtracted. The shares match the UK pattern: consumption 61%, government 26%, investment 14%, net trade −1%.

cards.front: Distinguish a movement along the AD curve from a shift of it.
cards.back: A movement along AD is caused only by a change in the average price level, other factors constant. A shift (AD1 to AD2) is caused by a change in any determinant other than the price level — C, I, G or X − M — changing total planned expenditure at every price level.
cards.svgAlt: Aggregate demand curve shifting right from AD1 to AD2, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 at price level PL

cards.front: Define disposable income, and state its role in consumption.
cards.back:
Disposable income — income available for spending after direct taxes, such as income tax, and after adding government transfer payments, such as benefits.

It is the primary determinant of consumption — households can only spend what they have available — and disposable income is split between consumption and saving.

cards.front: Define the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) and the marginal propensity to save (MPS).
cards.back:
MPC — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is spent on consumption. MPS — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is saved.

If a household spends £80 of an extra £100, the MPC is 0.8. A rise in the MPC means a fall in the MPS — every extra pound is either spent or saved.

cards.front: Beyond disposable income, what influences consumption?
cards.back:
• Interest rates — higher rates raise borrowing costs and the reward for saving, cutting consumption.
  • Consumer confidence — optimism about future income encourages spending and borrowing.
  • Wealth effects — rising house prices or share values encourage spending.
  • Income distribution — lower-income households have a higher MPC, so a more equal distribution raises total consumption.

cards.front: Distinguish gross from net investment, and define depreciation.
cards.back:
Gross investment — total spending on capital goods. Net investment — gross investment minus depreciation: the true addition to the capital stock, which is what raises productive potential.

Depreciation — the loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors. A firm spending £1m on machinery while £200,000 of capital wears out makes £800,000 of net investment.

cards.front: List the influences on investment in the Edexcel specification.
cards.back:
• The rate of economic growth — growth raises expected demand.
  • Business expectations and confidence — and Keynes' 'animal spirits': sentiment and intuition, not just calculation.
  • Demand for exports — export orders justify new capacity.
  • Interest rates — cheaper borrowing makes more projects viable.
  • Access to credit — willing lenders matter as much as the rate.
  • Government and regulations — tax incentives or restrictions.

cards.front: Explain the accelerator effect.
cards.back:
Investment depends on the change in the rate of economic growth, not its level. When growth accelerates, firms run short of capacity and must invest in new capital to meet the extra demand; when growth merely continues at the same rate, existing capacity suffices and investment need not rise at all.

This helps explain why investment is the most volatile component of AD.

cards.front: Explain the dual impact of investment on the economy.
cards.back:
Short run — investment is a component of AD, so more of it raises demand, stimulating growth and employment.

Long run — investment adds to the capital stock, raising the economy's productive potential and shifting LRAS right, which supports non-inflationary growth. The same spending works on both sides of the AD/AS diagram.

cards.front: What are the main influences on government expenditure?
cards.back:
The trade cycle — spending rises automatically in downturns as welfare claims grow, and falls in booms.

Fiscal policy — discretionary choices: expansionary policy raises G (infrastructure, education) to boost AD, growth and jobs; contractionary policy cuts G to cool inflation or close a deficit. Political priorities and demographics (an ageing population) shape the mix.

cards.front: Explain how automatic stabilisers work over the trade cycle.
cards.back:
Recession — welfare claims rise and tax revenues fall, so government spending rises automatically: a fiscal stimulus that supports AD without any policy decision.

Boom — welfare claims fall and tax revenues rise, so spending falls: an automatic contraction that cools the economy. The stabilisers dampen the cycle in both directions.

cards.front: Define net trade, and list its main influences.
cards.back:
Net trade — exports minus imports (X − M). A surplus (X > M) adds to aggregate demand; a deficit (X < M) subtracts from it.

Influences: real incomes at home and abroad, exchange rates, the state of the world economy, the degree of protectionism, and non-price factors such as quality, branding and innovation.

cards.front: How does a currency depreciation affect the trade balance? Name the two qualifications.
cards.back:
A depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, improving the trade balance — but only if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds: the combined price elasticities of demand for exports and imports must exceed one.

And not immediately: demand is inelastic in the short run, so the balance often worsens before improving — the J-curve effect, after the shape the trade balance traces over time.

cards.front: How do real incomes, the world economy and protectionism move the trade balance?
cards.back:
Real incomes — rising domestic incomes pull in imports (worsening); rising foreign incomes lift exports (improving). World economy — global growth lifts export demand, and for an open economy like the UK it is often the most important short-run driver.

Protectionism — tariffs and quotas cut imports, but invite retaliation against exports and raise prices at home. Non-price competitiveness — quality, branding and innovation decide who wins the trade that prices don't.
